newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers, issuers weigh in on IRS random audit plan.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers, issuers weigh in on IRS random audit plan.

text.p: Bond lawyers said they are surprised by IRS' plan to launch its random muni bond audit program in small issue industrial development bonds, but issuers said the move makes sense.
"It's a little strange," said Perry Israel, an attorney with Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe in San Francisco. "Small issue IDBs are a very small part of the municipal bond business.
Using that as a baseline to try to figure how to look at other bond issues may be difficult," Israel said.
But Catherine Spain, chief lobbyist for the Government Finance Officers Association, said small issue IDBs are exactly where "I would have expected them to target."
She said, "Look at where the defaults have been."
Spain and Israel were reacting to an announcement October 16 by Marcus Owens, head of Internal Revenue Service's exempt organizations division.

Owens told Reuters that under a work plan developed for the new random audit program, IRS will spend all of 1997 and the first quarter of 1998 examining about 100 IDB issues ranging from $1 million to $10 million in size.
But Floyd Newton, a bond lawyer with King & Spalding in Atlanta, said IRS could better target its time and scarce dollars.
"Years ago there was a boatload of stuff done in that area (IDBs), but now deals are few and far between," Newton said.
"It is like training auditors in a type of bond that is really a kind of dinosaur," said David Walton, a former attorney adviser in the U.S. Treasury Department's tax legislative counsel's office.

"Sure they are going to find som e people that violated" federal limits under the IDB program, said Walton, now a partner with Jones Hall Hill & White in San Fransisco. But, I don't think it's going to have a terribly significant effect on future behaviour," Walton said.
He said IRS should target limited resources at complicated, arbitrage-driven type transactions.
"Those type of transactions are where there are very close readings of the IRS code."
Israel said IRS would do better by focusing on multi-housing bond deals, airport financings or regular government bond issues.
Lawyers said IRS probably is focusing on IDBs because it has issued extensive technical guidance to examiners and issuers on the issue, including private letter rulings.
"It's an easy area to audit," said David Caprera, with Kutak Rock in Denver. "It's a very mechanical thing."
Israel said, "I, like many others, started out in the small issue area. Maybe it's agood place for IRS to start."
But Caprera said IRS will not get a real sense of muni-market compliance problems. It is like the "blind man who tries to describe the elephant by feeling its tail," he said.

Spain said IRS chose IDBs because it is sure to produce some tax violations. "Maybe they find (only) one or two, but it sends the message. You could look at a lot of general governments and not find anything," Spain said.
"Governments are really into compliance," Spain said. "IRS knows putting resourves in general government areas probably isn't going to yield very much."

Alan Anders, chairman of the regulatory committee of the Council of Infrastructure Financing Authorities, said IRS probably will find a larger percentage of violations in small issue IDBs than in other sectors.
"Where you have communities promoting economic development and where you've got small loans to small corporations, that's where you are going to see the biggest problems," said Anders.
Anders is director of finance policy for New York City Municipal Water Finance Authority and vice chairman of GFOA's governmental debt committee.
--Vicky Stamas, 202-898-8314
